Amazon's own annual report says it: $68.6 billion from adverts in 2025. Sponsored ads, display and video, all lumped together. That money comes from brands paying for the eye-level shelf, the spot in front of a shopper who is still deciding, still reading, still able to be nudged.

On Sunday 20 September, Amazon blocked a shopper who can't be nudged. Muse is Meta's AI helper that shops for people. Send it to buy a blender and it buys the blender. It doesn't stop to read the badge.

The next day, Shopify went the other way. Its boss, Tobi Lütke, posted on X that Shopify was "partnering deeply with Muse", so Muse can check out with Shop Pay, Shopify's one-tap checkout, on every Shopify store. He called it "an easy and delightful way to shop and check out with Muse."

Same robot shopper. Opposite answer. One shop threw it out. One held the door open. What does that tell you about who gets paid, and how?

## WHO GETS PAID

Think of Amazon as a giant supermarket. Brands pay Amazon to sit at eye level, the shelf a shopper sees first. That's the advertising money, all $68.6 billion of it. It only works if a person is walking the aisle, slowing down, glancing left and right.

Shopify is not the supermarket. Shopify is the till. It gets paid when you pay, through Shop Pay, its one-tap checkout. It doesn't care which shelf you picked things off. It cares that you're at the till.

Send a robot shopper down the aisle and it walks straight past eye level. It has a list. It doesn't glance sideways. That threatens the supermarket's shelf money. It does nothing to the till's fee.

Here's our guess, and it is a guess: a shopper that skips the shelf is a problem for Amazon and no problem at all for Shopify. That is why one blocked Muse and the other hugged it.

## WHAT THEY SAY

Amazon's stated reason has nothing to do with adverts. The popup shoppers saw read: "Continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon's Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed." Amazon's Conditions of Use are the rules you agree to just by using Amazon. Since May 2025 they've included "Agent Terms," which say no robot shopper may use Amazon "unless, at all times, it identifies itself." An Amazon spokesperson told CNET that apps that buy things for customers "should operate openly and respect service provider decisions about whether or not to participate." In plain English: tell us you're a robot, and ask first.

Amazon also told GeekWire that Muse doesn't identify itself when it browses, and appears to capture and store customer credentials. Meta said when it launched Muse that Muse "has no visibility into people's passwords or payment methods." When CNBC asked Meta to respond to the block, Meta declined to comment.

There's a second dispute running alongside this one, against a different company. In its court case against Perplexity, another AI company, Amazon filed an amended complaint on 21 September, in a court in California. Amazon wrote that its advertisers "pay for their ads to be shown to humans." It also claimed "lost advertising revenue attributable to non-human ad impressions" caused by Perplexity's shopping agent. The Fashion Law reported the complaint also says Perplexity "knowingly causes customers to violate Amazon's Conditions of Use." Those words were about Perplexity's robot, not Muse. Reading them across to Muse is our guess, not Amazon's claim.

Here's our guess, in full: Amazon's real worry is the $68.6 billion. A robot that doesn't glance at the shelf doesn't see the advert on it. Amazon has never said that sentence about Muse. We think it's true anyway.

Amazon's contract reason and our money guess sit right next to each other. Both are true because they are one move. The contract is the tool; the ad money is what it protects.

## WHAT DECIDES IT

Amazon's ad money is real today. The fixed thing that decides what happens next is already written down: Amazon's Conditions of Use.

Guess one. A judge in the Perplexity case reads those Agent Terms broadly. Amazon keeps every un-badged robot shopper off its shelves, for as long as it likes. Amazon wins. Every robot shopper, and everyone who built one, loses.

Guess two. Amazon opens a proper front door instead: robots welcome, so long as they identify themselves and behave. Amazon still shows them the eye-level shelf on the way through. Amazon keeps some ad money. Robot-makers get in from the cold.

Guess three. The court narrows the rule and robots simply route around Amazon, straight to Shopify's till instead. Shopify wins twice over. Amazon loses the shopper and never even gets to argue the point.

Our bet: guess two.

## OUR PREDICTION

By 30 June 2027, Amazon opens an authorised route for shopping agents, and that route still shows them sponsored listings.

How sure we are: 70%.
